pos: n. (William Tennent, 1673–1746, Irish-born Presbyterian minister in Pennsylvania, founder of the Log College)
etymology: Scots-Irish Tennent, a holder of land, from Latin tenere, to hold; William, Germanic, resolute protector.
biblical_def: William Tennent was educated in Ireland, ordained in the Church of Ireland, and came to Pennsylvania in 1718, where he was received by the Presbyterian synod and settled at Neshaminy in Bucks County. Finding the middle colonies starved of ministers and the available supply often unconverted, he built a log schoolhouse about twenty feet square beside his manse and taught young men the languages, logic and divinity, pressing on them above all the necessity of the new birth. Out of that building came his four sons, Samuel Blair, Samuel Finley, John Rowland and others — the preachers of the Great Awakening in the middle colonies. Whitefield visited in 1739 and described the place with affection; its detractors coined the name Log College in contempt and it stuck. The College of New Jersey, afterwards Princeton, is its direct descendant. 2Ti 2:2 is the whole method: commit what you have heard “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education; a school or academy in which young persons are instructed in the sciences or in theology; and to train, as to educate; to teach.
webster_full: SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.
TRAIN, v.t. To educate; to teach; to form by instruction or practice; to bring up.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college, and a common school.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
corruption_summary: A twenty-foot log hut beside a Bucks County manse produced the preachers of an awakening and, eventually, Princeton.
corruption_paragraphs: The Log College answers a question every generation faces: what does a church do when the ordinary pipeline of ministerial training has stopped producing converted men. Tennent's answer was neither to wait nor to denounce, but to start teaching. 2Ti 2:2 describes a chain of four links — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others also — and Tennent simply obeyed it at the scale available to him, with one room and a handful of students.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live failure is the assumption that ministerial formation requires institutional permission and a budget. Mat 9:38 commands prayer to the Lord of the harvest that He send forth labourers, and the praying church is ordinarily the one that ends up training them. Eph 4:11 says Christ gave pastors and teachers to the church; He gives them through men who take the trouble to teach.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit, to entrust; pistos (G4103), faithful; ekballo (G1544), to send forth.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to set before, to commit to one's charge; 2 Timothy 2:2.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to thrust out, to send forth; Matthew 9:38.
Greek poimen (G4166) — a shepherd, a pastor; Ephesians 4:11.
usage: “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the Log College method.
“that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38) — the prayer behind the school.
“how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — why a hut was worth building.

pos: n. (the log schoolhouse at Neshaminy, Pennsylvania, c. 1727–1746, where William Tennent trained ministers for the Great Awakening)
etymology: English log, a bulk of timber; college, from Latin collegium, a society of colleagues.
biblical_def: The Log College was one room of hewn logs, by report about twenty feet square, standing beside William Tennent's parsonage on the Neshaminy creek. In it, over roughly twenty years, perhaps twenty men were taught Latin, Greek, Hebrew, logic and theology, and were examined above all on whether they had passed from death to life. The graduates became the New Side party of the Presbyterian Church: Gilbert, William, John and Charles Tennent, Samuel Blair, Samuel Finley, John Rowland, William Robinson. Its opponents in the Philadelphia synod held that its degrees were worthless and tried to require a European or New England education for ordination, which was among the causes of the 1741 schism. The school closed at Tennent's death, and its spiritual descendants founded the College of New Jersey at Princeton in 1746. 2Ti 2:2 is the charter. Zec 4:6 is the comment on its appearance, for the outcome was not by might, nor by power.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a society of persons engaged in common pursuits, and an edifice appropriated to the use of students; and a log, as a bulk or mass of wood.
webster_full: COL'LEGE, n. A collection or assemblage; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits. An edifice appropriated to the use of students.
LOG, n. A bulk or mass of wood, unhewed; a piece of a tree cut or fallen.
ORDINA'TION, n. The act of conferring holy orders or sacerdotal power; the act of settling a Christian minister over a parish.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
corruption_summary: The synod said a log hut could not produce a minister, and then spent twenty years answering the men it produced.
corruption_paragraphs: The quarrel over the Log College was a quarrel about what qualifies a man for the ministry. The Philadelphia party was not wrong to want learning; the New Testament requires an elder apt to teach, and a man ignorant of the text cannot teach it. They were wrong to make a particular institution's certificate the test, and wrong to resist examining candidates on experimental godliness. 2Ti 2:2 names faithfulness and ability to teach, in that order, and says nothing about where the teaching was received.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern form of the same error is credentialism, where an accredited degree functions as the real ordination and the presbytery's examination becomes a formality. 1Co 1:23 is the standing reminder that the church's message is a stumblingblock and foolishness by the standards of the learned world, and that a training which makes a man ashamed of it has disqualified him however it is accredited.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to entrust; didaktikos, apt to teach; Hebrew koach (H3581), power.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit to one's charge; 2 Timothy 2:2.
usage: “commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — twenty men in twenty years.
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zec 4:6) — said of a log hut.
“we preach Christ crucified” (1Co 1:23) — the only curriculum that finally matters.

pos: n. (Gilbert Tennent, 1703–1764, Presbyterian minister at New Brunswick and Philadelphia, leader of the New Side in the Great Awakening)
etymology: Germanic Gisilberht, bright pledge; Tennent, a holder of land.
biblical_def: Gilbert Tennent was the eldest of William Tennent's sons and the fiercest preacher the middle colonies produced. Settled at New Brunswick in 1726, he fell into a near-fatal illness that left him resolved to spend himself on the unconverted, and he became Whitefield's chief ally in the American awakening. In March 1740 he preached at Nottingham the sermon that made and marred his reputation, The Danger of an Unconverted Ministry, from the text of the Pharisees as blind guides, charging that a minister who has not himself been born again cannot do a congregation good and that people under such a ministry may lawfully leave it. The Philadelphia synod expelled the New Brunswick presbytery the following year. Tennent afterwards regretted the sermon's severity and laboured for the reunion that came in 1758. John 3:3 is the doctrine the sermon pressed. Act 20:28 is the charge it applied, and 2Ti 2:2 the remedy his father had already built.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unconverted as not converted or changed in heart; not regenerate; and itinerant, as passing or traveling from place to place.
webster_full: UNCONVER'TED, a. Not converted; not changed in opinion. Not regenerated; not having a new heart.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or traveling from place to place; not settled; applied to preachers who travel.
SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church.
scriptures: John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: He was right that an unconverted ministry is a calamity and wrong to make every hearer the judge of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of the Nottingham sermon is biblical and the application overshot. Act 20:28 charges overseers to feed the church of God which He purchased with His own blood, and a man who has no part in that purchase cannot discharge the charge; John 10:11 distinguishes the shepherd who lays down his life from the hireling who flees. That much is plain. What Tennent added was that private hearers might judge the matter and withdraw at will, and the result was congregations split by rumour rather than by presbytery.

The modern corruption inverts the error. Where Tennent made conversion the ministry's test and overapplied it, much of the church has quietly dropped the test altogether, treating ministry as a profession entered by aptitude and training. John 3:3 applies to the man in the pulpit before it applies to anyone in the pews. The principle to recover is that examining a candidate's experience of grace is the presbytery's solemn duty, which is precisely why it is not every hearer's private errand.
roots_summary: Greek gennao (G1080), to be born; poimaino (G4165), to shepherd; misthotos (G3411), a hireling.
roots_lines: Greek gennao (G1080) — to be born, to beget; John 3:3.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend, to feed as a shepherd; Acts 20:28.
Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to purchase, to acquire; Acts 20:28.
usage: “Except a man be born again” (John 3:3) — applied first to the preacher.
“to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — the charge.
“the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11) — and the hireling does not.

pos: n. (the revival party in the American Presbyterian Church during the schism of 1741–1758, opposed to the Old Side)
etymology: English new, from Old English niwe; side, a party or faction.
biblical_def: The New Side were the Presbyterians of the middle colonies who received the Great Awakening: the Tennents, Samuel Blair, Samuel Finley, Samuel Davies and the New Brunswick presbytery. They held that the new birth is to be preached, pressed and discerned, that a candidate for the ministry must be examined on his experience of grace as well as his learning, and that itinerant preaching into another man's parish is lawful when souls are perishing in it. The Old Side answered that revival emotion was disorder, that presbytery boundaries bind, and that ordination requires a recognized education. The synod of Philadelphia expelled the New Brunswick men in 1741; the New Side founded the College of New Jersey, grew faster than their opponents, and the two sides reunited in 1758 on substantially New Side terms. John 3:3 was the party's rallying text. 1Co 14:40 was the Old Side's, and the dictionary holds that both verses are in the Bible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revival as renewed and more active attention to religion; an awakening of men to their spiritual concerns; and a schism, as a division or separation in a church.
webster_full: REVI'VAL, n. Renewed and more active attention to religion; an awakening of men to their spiritual concerns.
SCHISM, n. A division or separation in a church or denomination of Christians, occasioned by diversity of opinions.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or traveling from place to place; applied to preachers who travel.
scriptures: John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
corruption_summary: One party had the doctrine of the new birth and the other had the book of order, and the reunion needed both.
corruption_paragraphs: The schism is a case study in how two biblical commitments can be set against each other by men too tired to hold both. John 3:3 cannot be made optional; 1Co 14:40 cannot be made optional either. The New Side were right that a church which will not ask whether its ministers are converted has stopped being a church, and the Old Side were right that itinerants crossing presbytery lines without invitation leave wreckage behind them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Both errors are alive. Revivalist movements still treat church order as an obstacle to the Spirit, and confessional bodies still treat order as a substitute for life. Mat 9:37 says the harvest is plenteous and the labourers few, which is the New Side's urgency; Act 2:42 lists doctrine, fellowship, bread and prayers as the continuing shape of a church, which is the Old Side's stability. A healthy denomination does not choose.
roots_summary: Greek gennao (G1080), to be born; taxis (G5010), order; therismos (G2326), harvest.
roots_lines: Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer; Matthew 9:37.
usage: “Except a man be born again” (John 3:3) — the New Side's text.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Old Side's text.
“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — the urgency that caused the breach.

pos: n. (Samuel Blair, 1712–1751, Log College graduate, minister at Fagg's Manor, Pennsylvania, and chronicler of the awakening there)
etymology: Scottish Gaelic blàr, a plain or field; Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, heard of God.
biblical_def: Samuel Blair came from Ulster as a boy, was trained in William Tennent's Log College, and in 1739 took the congregation at Fagg's Manor in Chester County, where he opened a classical school of his own. Samuel Davies, John Rodgers and Alexander Cumming were taught there. In 1740 a powerful awakening broke out under his preaching, and the narrative he wrote of it four years later is among the soberest first-hand accounts of such a season: he records the outcries and faintings without celebrating them, distinguishes conviction from conversion, and insists that the test is a changed life afterwards. He wrote for the New Side in the schism and died at thirty-nine. Act 2:42 supplies his test, a people continuing stedfastly. Jas 1:27 supplies another, religion visible in mercy and in keeping unspotted. John 3:3 is what he preached for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conviction, in theology, as the act of convincing of sin; and awakening, as rousing from sleep or indifference, particularly in religious concerns.
webster_full: CONVIC'TION, n. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge; the state of being convinced or convicted by conscience.
AWA'KENING, n. A revival of religion, or more general attention to religion, than usual.
NAR'RATIVE, n. The recital of a story; a continued account of the particulars of an event or transaction.
scriptures: John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
corruption_summary: Blair wrote down what happened in his parish without exaggerating it, which is rarer in revival literature than revival.
corruption_paragraphs: Revival narratives tend to one of two failures: they inflate, or they are written by critics who deny anything happened. Blair does neither. He reports the physical effects because they occurred and refuses to treat them as evidence of grace, directing his readers instead to what the awakened persons were like a year later. Act 2:42 gives the test he used, a company continuing stedfastly in doctrine, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation it names is the measuring of a ministry by responses rather than by fruit. Jas 1:27 locates pure religion in the care of the fatherless and the widow and in personal holiness, neither of which is visible on the night of a meeting. Pro 11:30 calls the winner of souls wise, and wisdom here includes the patience to wait and see.
roots_summary: Greek gennao (G1080), to be born; proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly; threskeia (G2356), religion.
usage: “Except a man be born again” (John 3:3) — what Fagg's Manor was preached for.
“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42) — his test, applied a year later.
“to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27) — the fruit he looked for.

pos: n. (Samuel Davies, 1723–1761, evangelist of Virginia Presbyterianism, hymnwriter, President of the College of New Jersey)
etymology: Welsh patronymic, son of David; Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, heard of God.
biblical_def: Samuel Davies was trained at Samuel Blair's school at Fagg's Manor and sent in 1747 as an evangelist to Hanover County, Virginia, where the established church held the ground and dissenters preached by licence or not at all. He secured licences for seven meeting houses, argued the legal case for toleration under the Act of Toleration before the General Court, and built the first Presbyterian presbytery in the colony. He catechized and taught slaves to read so that they could read the Scriptures, baptized many, and left accounts of their singing that are among the earliest notices of African-American Christian worship. In 1753 he sailed with Gilbert Tennent to raise money in Britain for the College of New Jersey, and became its president in 1759, dying eighteen months later at thirty-seven. Rom 10:14 drove the whole: how shall they hear without a preacher. Act 26:18 names the commission he worked under, to turn men from darkness to light.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an evangelist as a preacher or publisher of the gospel; and toleration, as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
webster_full: EVAN'GELIST, n. A writer of the history of Jesus Christ; a preacher or publisher of the gospel of Jesus Christ.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.
CAT'ECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: He won legal room for dissenters in Virginia and spent it teaching slaves to read the Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: Davies is the answer to the claim that colonial Reformed Christianity had nothing to say to the enslaved. He taught reading because Psa 119:130 is true, that the entrance of God's words giveth light and giveth understanding unto the simple, and a man who cannot read cannot enter them for himself. He baptized on profession after examination, the same standard he applied to planters, which in that society was itself a statement.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest thing to say is that Davies did not call for abolition and that the dictionary does not pretend he did. What he did was refuse the premise on which the whole system leaned, that these were not souls to be addressed. Act 26:18 commissions the turning of men from darkness to light and from the power of Satan unto God, and it names no exempt category. The principle to recover is that literacy in the Scriptures is a missionary act.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach; epistrepho (G1994), to turn; Hebrew pethach (H6608), opening, entrance.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, to preach; Romans 10:14.
Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to convert; Acts 26:18.
Hebrew pethach (H6608) — an opening, an entrance; Psalm 119:130.
usage: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the Hanover mission in a question.
“to turn them from darkness to light” (Act 26:18) — the commission, with no exemptions.
“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — why he taught reading.

pos: n. (Joseph Bellamy, 1719–1790, Connecticut pastor at Bethlehem, pupil of Jonathan Edwards, founder of the New Divinity school)
etymology: Norman French bel ami, fair friend; Joseph, from Hebrew Yoseph, he shall add.
biblical_def: Joseph Bellamy studied divinity in Jonathan Edwards' house at twenty, settled at Bethlehem in Connecticut, and stayed fifty years, training perhaps sixty ministers in what was effectively the first Protestant theological seminary in America: men lodged with him, read, and were examined. His True Religion Delineated of 1750, for which Edwards wrote the preface, pressed the distinction between a religion of self-interest and a religion of love to God for what He is. With Samuel Hopkins he developed the system called the New Divinity, which held the governmental theory of the atonement, taught that the sinner's inability is moral and not natural, and denied that there are any exercises of the unregenerate which God requires as preparatory. The dictionary values his pastoral seriousness and rejects the governmental atonement. Rom 5:1 and Rom 3:28 keep justification forensic; Gal 2:20 makes the substitution personal, for Christ “loved me, and gave himself for me.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines atonement as expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury; and disinterested, as free from selfish motive.
webster_full: ATO'NEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
DISIN'TERESTED, a. Free from self-interest; having no personal interest or private advantage in a question.
BENEV'OLENCE, n. The disposition to do good; good will; kindness; charitableness.
scriptures: Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead:
corruption_summary: Bellamy trained sixty ministers in his parsonage and bent the doctrine of the atonement while doing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The governmental theory holds that Christ's death was not the payment of the elect's debt but a public demonstration by which God could forgive without His moral government being despised. It sounds reverent and it loses the thing that makes the gospel good news. Rom 3:28 and Rom 5:1 speak of justification, a courtroom verdict grounded in a real satisfaction, and Gal 2:20 makes that satisfaction personal and particular: He loved me and gave Himself for me, not for an abstraction.

The New Divinity's pastoral instinct was not contemptible. Bellamy and Hopkins were fighting a dead formalism in which men rested on covenant privileges and the Half-Way arrangement, and 2Co 5:14 is a verse they loved, that the love of Christ constraineth us. But a defective atonement cannot sustain the disinterested love they demanded, because that love is a response to a debt actually paid. Later New England theology drifted from Bellamy toward a moral influence that kept the governmental scaffolding and lost the cross.
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; hilasterion (G2435), propitiation; sunecho (G4912), to constrain.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to justify; Romans 5:1.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to conclude; Romans 3:28.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to give over, to deliver up; Galatians 2:20.
Greek sunecho (G4912) — to hold together, to constrain; 2 Corinthians 5:14.
usage: “being justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Rom 5:1) — a verdict, not a demonstration.
“who loved me, and gave himself for me” (Gal 2:20) — particular and personal.
“the love of Christ constraineth us” (2Co 5:14) — the New Divinity's favourite text.

pos: n. (Samuel Hopkins, 1721–1803, pastor at Great Barrington and Newport, systematizer of the New Divinity, early American abolitionist)
etymology: English patronymic, little Hob, from Robert; Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, heard of God.
biblical_def: Samuel Hopkins boarded in Jonathan Edwards' house as a young graduate, served a frontier parish at Great Barrington, and from 1770 pastored the First Congregational Church at Newport, Rhode Island — the busiest slave port in North America. He preached against the trade to a congregation that profited from it, lost members and salary for it, addressed the Continental Congress on it in 1776, and worked to send freed Africans as missionaries to Africa. His System of Doctrines of 1793 carried Edwards' theology into the shape called Hopkinsianism: disinterested benevolence as the essence of holiness, sin as a necessary means to the greatest good, and a willingness to be damned for the glory of God as the mark of true submission. The dictionary rejects those last two and honours the first life in America to cost a minister his living over slavery. 2Co 5:14 is his text. Jas 1:27 is his record. Rom 3:28 is where his system went wrong by making holiness rather than Christ the ground of acceptance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines benevolence as the disposition to do good; good will; and abolition, as the act of abolishing; the putting an end to.
webster_full: BENEV'OLENCE, n. The disposition to do good; good will; kindness; charitableness; the love of mankind, accompanied with a desire to promote their happiness.
ABOLI'TION, n. The act of abolishing; or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation.
SUBMIS'SION, n. The act of submitting; the act of yielding to power or authority.
scriptures: For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead:
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
corruption_summary: He preached against the slave trade in the town that ran it, and built a system in which a man should be willing to be damned.
corruption_paragraphs: The willingness-to-be-damned test is the clearest error in Hopkins, and it comes from a true premise pushed past Scripture. God's glory is indeed the highest end, and 2Co 5:14 is right that the love of Christ constrains. But Scripture never requires a believer to be indifferent to his own salvation; it commands him to make his calling and election sure, and Gal 2:20 roots his whole life in the assurance that the Son of God loved him and gave Himself for him. A test no apostle applied is not a mark of holiness.

Nor can disinterested benevolence be the ground of acceptance. Rom 3:28 concludes that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, and holiness — however disinterested — is a deed. Where Hopkins was magnificently right was Jas 1:27: he visited the afflicted in the one way his town could not forgive. The principle to recover is that a defective system did not stop God using a faithful man, and that his courage is not an argument for his theology.
roots_summary: Greek sunecho (G4912), to constrain; threskeia (G2356), religion; dikaioo (G1344), to justify.
roots_lines: Greek sunecho (G4912) — to constrain, to press together; 2 Corinthians 5:14.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to conclude; 2 Corinthians 5:14.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, to look after; James 1:27.
usage: “the love of Christ constraineth us” (2Co 5:14) — preached in a slave port.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — what it cost him.
“a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) — where the system failed.

pos: n. (the theological school descended from Jonathan Edwards through Bellamy and Hopkins, dominant in New England Congregationalism c. 1760–1830)
etymology: English new; divinity, from Latin divinitas, the science of divine things.
biblical_def: The New Divinity, also called Hopkinsianism or the New England Theology, was the first indigenous American school of systematic theology. Taking Jonathan Edwards as its head, it was built by Joseph Bellamy and Samuel Hopkins and carried on by Jonathan Edwards the younger, Nathanael Emmons and Timothy Dwight. Its marks were the distinction between natural and moral inability, the governmental theory of the atonement, disinterested benevolence as the essence of true virtue, the denial of means of grace available to the unregenerate, and a doctrine of sin as the necessary means of the greatest good. It produced rigorous preaching, a generation of missionaries and the first American seminaries, and it also ground down the Reformed doctrine of imputation until its successors could dispense with it. The dictionary values the seriousness and names the defect. Rom 3:28 and Rom 5:1 keep justification forensic. Eph 2:8 and Eph 2:9 keep salvation a gift, not of works, lest any man should boast.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines divinity as the science of divine things; theology; and imputation, as the act of imputing or charging; attribution.
webster_full: DIVIN'ITY, n. The science of divine things; theology; the science which unfolds the character of God, his laws and moral government.
IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; generally in an ill sense.
INABIL'ITY, n. Want of power or capacity; weakness; impotence.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: A school built to defend Edwards ended by handing his grandchildren the tools to dismantle him.
corruption_paragraphs: The instructive thing about the New Divinity is how a movement of unquestioned earnestness drifted. Each adjustment was defended as a clarification: inability restated as moral rather than natural so that the sinner's guilt is plain; the atonement restated as governmental so that God's justice is vindicated without a commercial calculus; imputation softened so that no man is punished for another's act. Each step was taken in good faith and the cumulative result was a New England theology from which Finney and then Unitarianism could be reached without a violent break.

Eph 2:8 and Eph 2:9 are the two verses the drift could not accommodate: salvation by grace through faith, the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast. A system in which the essence of holiness is disinterested benevolence has put a human disposition where Scripture puts a gift. Rom 5:1 makes peace with God the fruit of a verdict already rendered, and a verdict rests on an imputed righteousness or on nothing at all.
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; charis (G5485), grace; doron (G1435), a gift.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to justify, to declare righteous; Romans 3:28.
usage: “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) — the verse the system strained.
“by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8) — a gift, not a disposition.
“Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9) — where benevolence cannot stand.

pos: n. (Timothy Dwight, 1752–1817, President of Yale College, preacher of the Second Great Awakening in New England, grandson of Jonathan Edwards)
etymology: English Dwight, from the personal name Diot; Timothy, from Greek Timotheos, honouring God.
biblical_def: Timothy Dwight entered Yale at thirteen, served as an army chaplain in the Revolution, pastored at Greenfield Hill, and in 1795 became President of Yale, which he found in the grip of a fashionable infidelity — students reportedly called one another Voltaire and Rousseau. Rather than forbidding the reading, he invited the senior class to debate whether the Scriptures are the word of God, let them make the deist case at length, and answered it in a series of addresses afterwards published. Within a few years Yale saw successive seasons of revival, and a third of the student body professed conversion in 1802. His sermons were gathered as Theology Explained and Defended, a moderate New Divinity. 1Pe 3:15 is the method exactly: ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason of the hope that is in you. 2Ti 4:2 adds the persistence, and Act 17:11 the confidence that honest examination serves the truth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infidelity as disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine original of Christianity; and apologetics, the defense of Christianity.
webster_full: INFIDEL'ITY, n. Disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine original of christianity; unbelief.
DE'ISM, n. The doctrine or creed of a deist; the belief or system of religious opinions of those who acknowledge the existence of one God, but deny revelation.
DEFENSE', n. That which opposes attack, violence, danger or injury; vindication; justification.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Dwight let the Yale seniors argue for deism at full strength and then answered them, and the college was awakened.
corruption_paragraphs: The method is worth more than the man's theology, which was a moderated New Divinity the dictionary does not follow at every point. Dwight assumed that the truth gains by examination and that students forbidden to state an objection will simply hold it unanswered. 1Pe 3:15 commands an answer, which presupposes that the question has been heard, and commands it with meekness and fear, which rules out contempt for the questioner.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live failure is on both sides. Christian institutions still try to keep objections out rather than answer them, which produces graduates whose faith collapses on first contact; and the wider academy has abandoned the premise Dwight and his deist students shared, that the question has an answer and argument can reach it. Act 17:11 commends searching the Scriptures daily to see whether the things were so, and Isa 8:20 supplies the standard the search answers to.
roots_summary: Greek apologia (G627), a defence; elpis (G1680), hope; anakrino (G350), to examine.
roots_lines: Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, an answer; 1 Peter 3:15.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; Acts 17:11.
Greek elegcho (G1651) — to reprove, to convict; 2 Timothy 4:2.
usage: “be ready always to give an answer to every man” (1Pe 3:15) — the Yale debates.
“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — the premise.
“reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2) — and then the answer.
